headline: Operator RegExp patterns are matched against the whole value: form validation and CORS origins
summary: Two places matched an operator-supplied RegExp with an unanchored `.test()`, where a whole-string match was expected. `b.forms.validate` tested a field's `pattern` unanchored, so a value that merely contained a match passed server-side even though the browser rejects it: the same pattern is rendered as the HTML5 `pattern=` attribute, which the browser anchors over the entire value, so `pattern: /[0-9]{4}/` accepted `"12345"` (and `/[a-z]{3}/` accepted `"abc; DROP TABLE users"`) on the server while the client refused them. Server-side validation now anchors the pattern to the whole value (`^(?:source)$`, preserving flags), matching the browser and closing the client/server divergence. Separately, `b.middleware.cors` reflected a matched Origin into `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`, so a RegExp origin that admitted more hosts than intended leaked responses to an attacker origin: an unanchored `/example\.com/` matched `https://example.com.attacker.test`, and with `credentials:true` a pattern like `/^https:\/\/.*\.com$/` reflected any registrable `.com` origin with `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`. Because no finite check can prove an arbitrary RegExp is host-specific, `create()` now refuses a RegExp origin outright when `credentials:true` (use exact string origins for credentialed CORS); for `credentials:false` it requires whole-origin anchoring and rejects catch-all patterns, and matching consumes the entire origin. Separately, `b.network.tls.ocsp.buildRequest` built the RFC 6960 CertID lookup hash with SHA-1; it now defaults to SHA-256, with a `certIdHashAlg` opt to downgrade for a responder that only indexes SHA-1 CertIDs.

items.title: b.forms.validate anchors a field pattern to the whole submitted value
items.body: A field `pattern` is rendered verbatim as the HTML5 `pattern=` attribute, which the browser compiles anchored over the entire value. Server-side, `b.forms.validate` ran `pattern.test(value)` unanchored, so it accepted a value that only contained a match even though the browser rejects that value. An attacker bypassing the client (or any non-browser client) could submit `"12345"` against `pattern: /[0-9]{4}/`, or trailing payload past a short pattern, and pass server validation. Validation now matches the pattern against the whole value (`^(?:source)$`, preserving the `i`/`s`/`u` flags and dropping `g`/`y`/`m`), so the server and the browser agree. A pattern already written as `^...$` is unaffected.

items.title: b.middleware.cors refuses a RegExp origin with credentials, and matches non-credentialed RegExp origins against the whole origin
items.body: Origin matching runs `pattern.test(origin)` and reflects a matched Origin into `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`. A credentialed CORS response reflecting a pattern-matched origin leaks authenticated responses to any host the RegExp admits, and an arbitrary RegExp cannot be proven host-specific: `/^https:\/\/.*\.com$/` trusts every registrable `.com`, and a scheme, port, or IP-form wildcard evades any finite probe. `create()` now throws `cors/regex-origin-with-credentials` when a RegExp origin is paired with `credentials:true`; use exact string origins for credentialed CORS. For `credentials:false`, where no credentials are reflected, RegExp origins are still allowed but must match the whole origin: `create()` throws `cors/unanchored-pattern` for a pattern not anchored at both ends (`^...$`) and `cors/overbroad-pattern` for a catch-all, matching consumes the entire origin (so an internally half-anchored alternation cannot substring-match), and the previous ReDoS screening remains. Anchor RegExp origins to the complete origin, for example `/^https:\/\/([a-z0-9-]+\.)?example\.com$/`.

items.title: b.network.tls.ocsp.buildRequest builds the CertID with SHA-256 by default
items.body: The OCSP request CertID (`issuerNameHash` + `issuerKeyHash`, RFC 6960 §4.1.1) was built with SHA-1. It is a lookup key, not an integrity check (the response is bound by the responder's signature, not this hash), but shipping SHA-1 draws a weak-algorithm finding and SHA-256 is the stricter default. `buildRequest` now defaults the CertID hash to SHA-256, and accepts `certIdHashAlg` (`sha256` | `sha384` | `sha512` | `sha1`, listed in `b.network.tls.ocsp.CERTID_HASH_ALGS`) so an operator whose responder indexes revocation only by a SHA-1 CertID can opt down explicitly. `undefined` or `null` selects the default; any other value, including an empty string, throws `tls/ocsp-bad-certid-hash-alg`. `b.network.tls.ocsp.fetch` forwards the option, and `b.cert.create` accepts it as `ocsp.certIdHashAlg` for stapling refreshes. `b.cert.create` validates the value when the manager is created and throws `cert/bad-ocsp-certid-hash-alg` for an unsupported one; a refresh records its failure only as an audit event, so a misspelled value accepted at create time would leave the server running without fresh staples. The verifier already reads the hashAlgorithm from the response CertID and recomputes with it, so a SHA-256 request round-trips against a conforming responder with no other change.
